The Multiplier: Spending That Echoes

In micro, the link from my spending to your income stays invisible. In macro, that link is what moves the whole economy.

When the government pays to build a bridge, the 🧑 workers earn income. They spend most of what they earn. That spending becomes someone else's income. So spending echoes around and grows bigger than it started. The more of each won people spend, the bigger the echo. That growth factor is the multiplier in the formula below.

For example, say you spend 1,000 won on snacks at the corner 🏪 shop. The owner uses that 💰 money to buy supplies next door. The next owner spends it again somewhere else. Your 1,000 won travels around the neighborhood, getting spent again and again. The neighborhood earns far more than your first 1,000 won.

Examples & Exercises

The government spends 101010 more on a bridge, and the marginal propensity to consume is c=0.8c = 0.8c=0.8.

How much does income rise in total?

Show proof

  1. The 101010 paid for the bridge becomes the workers' income, and they spend 80%80\%80% of it — 888. That 888 becomes the shopkeepers' income, and 6.46.46.4 of it is spent again: spending turns into income, income into spending.

  2. Adding up every round gives 10+8+6.4+⋯=101−0.8=5010 + 8 + 6.4 + \cdots = \frac{10}{1 - 0.8} = 5010+8+6.4+⋯=1−0.810​=50. Five times the initial 101010: income climbs from 210210210 to 260260260.

Which grows income more: cutting taxes by 101010, or raising government spending by 101010? (c=0.8c = 0.8c=0.8)

Show proof

  1. A tax cut of 101010 raises disposable income by 101010, but only 80%80\%80% of it — 888 — is actually spent in the first round; the other 222 leaks straight into saving. Extra spending puts the full 101010 to work from round one.

  2. So the tax cut delivers 81−0.8=40\frac{8}{1 - 0.8} = 401−0.88​=40, exactly one first round less than the 505050 from spending. That is why the tax multiplier −c1−c=−4-\frac{c}{1-c} = -4−1−cc​=−4 is exactly 111 smaller in absolute value than the spending multiplier 555.
